analysis.one_liner: Extends and expands government health insurance for low-income children, letting states cover families up to triple the poverty line.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee and received no vote before the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have reauthorized the Children's Health Insurance Program for five years, appropriating steadily rising federal funding so states would not run short and enrolled children would not lose coverage. It let states cover children in families earning up to 300% of the poverty line, created an "Express Lane" so other agencies' records could be used to enroll kids without new paperwork, and required dental and mental health coverage. It also gave states new options to cover pregnant women and legal-immigrant children.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income uninsured children — about 9 million at the time, roughly 7 in 10 of whom were already eligible for CHIP or Medicaid but not enrolled — plus targeted low-income pregnant women and legal-immigrant children in states that take up the new options. Families get dental and mental health benefits added to required coverage, and states facing funding shortfalls get automatic reallocation so enrolled children are not dropped.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income uninsured children and pregnant women

how_it_helps.text: Appropriates rising federal CHIP funding from $8.5 billion in FY2008 to $15.4 billion in FY2012, replacing a financing structure the bill's findings said left nearly 2 million enrolled children at risk of losing coverage over five years.
Gives states the option to cover children in families with income up to 300% of the poverty line, with extra conditions imposed on states wanting to go higher.

Creates an "Express Lane" option letting states use income and citizenship determinations already made by agencies like school lunch or food stamp programs to enroll children, cutting the procedural denials the bill said affected many eligible children.
Requires CHIP coverage of dental and mental health services and lets states cover targeted low-income pregnant women and legal-immigrant children.
Establishes a quarterly reallocation process that moves unused federal funds to states facing projected CHIP shortfalls, so children do not lose coverage because of state-by-state funding mismatches.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through appropriations totaling roughly $58 billion over FY2008–FY2012. The bill text provided does not specify an offsetting revenue source. Private insurers also bear a competitive cost where expanded public eligibility draws children out of commercial coverage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; private insurers at the margin

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates about $58 billion over five years with no pay-for specified in the introduced text, so the cost would fall on federal taxpayers and the deficit unless separate revenue was enacted.

Raising eligibility to 300% of the poverty line invites substitution: some children with access to employer or private coverage could shift to public coverage, raising public costs without reducing the uninsured count as much as claimed — a standard objection to CHIP expansions at higher income levels.
Making proof-of-citizenship documentation a state option could loosen verification in some states, a tradeoff critics of the 2005 documentation requirement flagged as a program-integrity concern.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The spending is large but the targeting is defensible: most of the money goes to children who are already eligible but blocked by enrollment barriers, and to states about to run out of money for children already enrolled. The bill builds in guardrails — states wanting to go above 300% of poverty must first show low-income uninsured rates below the national average and streamlined enrollment. The main honest criticism is the absence of a specified funding source in the introduced text.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in April 2007 with bipartisan sponsorship, it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Senator Rockefeller introduced the bill on April 25, 2007, joined by Senator Snowe and Senator Kennedy as the bill's original co-introducers.
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has jurisdiction over Medicaid and CHIP.
The bill attracted 22 cosponsors, including 2 Republicans and independent members.
The only further entries in the action history are two rounds of sponsor introductory remarks, in April and July 2007; the Finance Committee never reported the bill and the Senate never voted on it.
CHIP was ultimately reauthorized early in the next Congress by separate legislation, after the 110th Congress's expansion bills were blocked and, in the House-passed case, vetoed.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the short term, opponents of a larger federal role in children's health coverage — including a president who vetoed the expansion versions that did reach his desk — were better off, since no expanded reauthorization became law in this Congress. States and clinics serving CHIP children got no new funding formula from this bill, though Congress did reauthorize the program early in the next Congress, so enrolled children did not simply lose coverage.

against.what_they_did: The Finance Committee, which he chaired, never scheduled a markup or reported the bill; it sat there for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: George W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Opposed CHIP expansion and vetoed the similar CHIP reauthorization expansions that passed Congress in 2007, setting the terms of the fight this bill was part of.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 22 cosponsors including 2 Republicans and independent members, plus a Republican original co-introducer — though the larger 2007 CHIP expansion fight split mostly by party, with both chambers passing expansions that a Republican president vetoed.

industries.note: Expanding public eligibility to 300% of the poverty line would pull some children out of commercial coverage, so carriers generally opposed expansions. But most CHIP benefits are delivered through contracts with private managed-care plans, so the same expansion would route more public dollars to the plans that hold state CHIP contracts.
More covered children means more paid care, and the bill's required dental and mental health benefits specifically channel new spending to those providers.
The bill sends states larger, more predictable federal funding, automatic reallocation when they face shortfalls, and 75% federal matching for eligibility IT and translation services.
